newsitem.title: POLAND: NO TAX WRITE-OFFS IN POLISH PRIVATE PENSION FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: NO TAX WRITE-OFFS IN POLISH PRIVATE PENSION FUNDS.

text.p: The Polish finance ministry said on Wednesday it planned no tax deduction for contributions voluntary, private pension schemes after the planned reform of the social security system.
"It has been decided that this solution (the tax write-off) would not be justified," deputy finance minister Waldemar Manugiewicz told a news conference.
Government officials earlier said that a proposal to offer some tax reliefs for those saving in private pension schemes, such as in those provided by insurance companies, had been considered.
Under the social security reform, currently discussed by the government, private, voluntary pension schemes are to be a supplementary source of income after retirement.

The main pension will come from two other sources -- the state-owned Social Security Office (ZUS), now the sole pension provider, and new planned funds, contributions to which would mandatory and tax-deductible.

While ZUS will continue to immediately spend all premiums its collects on state-regulated pensions, the new funds -- independent but supervised by the government -- would invest premiums in securities to make future individual benefits as high as possible.

Manugiewicz said that because premiums to the fully private pension schemes would not be tax deductible, pensions from this source would be tax free. But pensions from ZUS and the new funds would be taxed on the general basis.
The new funds, likely to be launched in 1999 if parliament passes relevant laws before this year's parliamentary polls, would be exempted from the corporate tax, Manugiewicz said.

The new funds will get part of the premium now paid to ZUS, which amounts to 45 percent of the salary, while the state subsidy for ZUS will increase. The increase would be financed from privatisation revenues.

The pension reform also envisages the creation of corporate pension funds, yet another source of income for retired people, to which employers, upon an agreement with workers, would contribute up to seven percent of employers' taxable income.
Premiums to the industrial funds would be tax deductible but stipends provided by them would be taxed. -- Marcin Grajewski +48 22 653 9700
